meta.title: Who really said "The healthiest competition occurs when average people win by putting in above-average effort"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Colin Powell is credited with this line everywhere, but no page of My American Journey — or any speech — has ever been cited. What the record actually shows.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The healthiest competition occurs when average people win by putting in above-average effort'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Colin Powell since at least 2004 — but the My American Journey citation has never come with a page. The honest state of the evidence.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2021 · U.S. Army general, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and 65th Secretary of State
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Colin Powell, and squarely in the register of the plain leadership maxims he was known for. But no primary source pins this exact wording: the memoir My American Journey is named by several quote sites without a page, chapter or edition, and the line was already circulating uncredited on quote aggregators by June 2004.

source.heading: What the record actually shows

docMeta.dd: None — no page, chapter or edition, in any source located
A quote-site page archived 12 June 2004, crediting Powell with no work named

source.excerpt: The healthiest competition occurs when average people win by putting in above-average effort.
trail: The line was circulating with nothing attached to it well before it reached any reference work: the Internet Archive’s 12 June 2004 capture of BrainyQuote’s Colin Powell page ↗ gives it under his name alone — no book, no speech, no date.

Wikiquote first carried the sentence on 29 January 2008 ↗, dropped into a flat “Sourced” list with no citation line of its own — while the two memoir quotations immediately below it each carried a “My American Journey” sub-bullet.
On the current Wikiquote page ↗ the line now sits beneath a “My American Journey (1996)” heading, still with no page, chapter or edition. The heading is the only thing tying it to the book.

The memoir is real and easy to check — My American Journey, by Colin L. Powell with Joseph E. Persico, Random House, 1995 ↗. A full-text search of the scanned copy was not possible for this review: the Internet Archive’s search-inside service was returning errors on 18 August 2026, so the memoir is neither confirmed nor excluded here.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller original context to show. Every version located is the sentence standing alone on a quotation page — never a paragraph, never a page number, never a transcript.

source.rightsNote: No work has been tied to this wording, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted. If the sentence does come from My American Journey (Random House, 1995), it is firmly in copyright to Powell’s estate and his publisher; if it originated in a speech or an interview it is later still. Nothing here supports treating it as public domain.

author.heading: About Colin Powell
author.metaLine: 1937–2021 · U.S. Army general · Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff 1989–1993 · Secretary of State 2001–2005
author.bio: Born in Harlem on 5 April 1937, Colin Powell rose through the U.S. Army to become Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in 1989 and, in 2001, the 65th Secretary of State — the first Black American to hold either post. He told his own story in My American Journey (1995, written with Joseph E. Persico) and returned to the subject of leadership in It Worked for Me (2012). He was known for compressing hard-won management sense into short, quotable rules — which is exactly why unsourced maxims drift toward his name.

misattribution.heading: The citation problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody else claims this sentence — the trouble is the source that travels with it. Every version located credits Powell; none produces a page.

items.why: Several aggregators attach the memoir to the line — AZQuotes gives “My American Journey (1995), Random House Incorporated” ↗ — but with no page, chapter or edition. A book title without a page is a label, not a citation.

When the line first appeared on Wikiquote on 29 January 2008 ↗ it carried no citation at all, while the neighbouring memoir quotations each carried a “My American Journey” sub-bullet. It sits under the book’s heading today, but no page was ever supplied for it.

The most-copied form drops the “in” and the hyphen, leaving an ungrammatical sentence — that is the form already in circulation in June 2004 ↗ and the form Goodreads still shows ↗. The cleaner “putting in above-average effort” is what Wikiquote prints ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit it to Powell if you like — nothing contradicts it — but do not credit it to a page of My American Journey. No source located, Wikiquote included, supplies one ↗.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to pin
lead: Powell is one of the great magnets for orphan maxims, and for an understandable reason: he really did talk that way. His leadership rules were short, blunt and built to be repeated, so a stray line in that voice finds a comfortable home under his name and stays there.

What makes this one worth flagging is not doubt about Powell — it is how confidently a source appears out of nowhere. The line shows up uncredited on a quote site in 2004, reaches Wikiquote in 2008 still uncredited, and is later reorganised under a book heading. Downstream sites copy the heading as though it were a citation, and a book title with no page starts circulating as proof.
detailsBody: Two checks that would settle this were unavailable on 18 August 2026: the Internet Archive’s search-inside service was returning server errors, and the Google Books API was over its daily quota. So the memoir is neither confirmed nor ruled out here — anyone with a physical copy of My American Journey and a good index could close this question in a few minutes.

No competing claimant surfaced in this review, and Quote Investigator has no entry for the line. That absence is why this page says “attributed” rather than “disputed”: there is no evidence the credit is wrong, only no evidence that it is right.
context.pull: A book title without a page is a label, not a citation.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Colin Powell page lists "The healthiest competition occurs when average people win by putting in above-average effort." under a "My American Journey (1996)" heading, with no page, chapter or edition given for that line.

The Wikiquote revision of 29 January 2008 contains the line placed in a flat "Sourced" list with no citation sub-bullet, while the two adjacent memoir quotations each carry a "'My American Journey', Colin Powell's autobiography" sub-bullet.

BrainyQuote's Colin Powell page, as captured by the Internet Archive on 12 June 2004, carries "The healthiest competition occurs when average people win by putting above average effort." credited to Colin Powell with no work, speech or date named.
The Internet Archive catalog record identifies My American Journey as by Colin L. Powell and Joseph E. Persico, published New York: Random House, 1995, ISBN 0679432965 / 9780679432968.

The Goodreads quote page shows the wording "...by putting above average effort." credited only to "Colin Powell" with no book cited, alongside the notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.
AZQuotes displays the quote with the source line "My American Journey (1995), Random House Incorporated" and no page number.

Colin Powell was born 5 April 1937 in Harlem, New York City, died 18 October 2021, served as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff from 1 October 1989 to 30 September 1993 and as Secretary of State from 20 January 2001 to 26 January 2005; his memoir My American Journey was published in 1995.
